issues.description: Deprecation correctly removes incidental wrapper that complected two redirects into one signature.
issues.detail: redirected() complected stdout and stderr redirection into a single tuple-argument context manager when the stdlib already offers two composable, single-purpose context managers. Removing it is a move toward simple-not-easy: two decomposed pieces replacing one combined convenience. The PR is doing the right kind of subtraction.

issues.description: Deprecation message omits how to replace the combined stdout+stderr case.
issues.detail: The old function let callers redirect both streams in one with-block. The new guidance is two stdlib calls, which users must nest or ExitStack. The deprecation string should say so explicitly, otherwise users will reach for the easy (familiar) thing rather than the simple (decomposed) one. A one-line example would close the gap.

issues.description: Deprecation test asserts behavior of code already scheduled for removal.
issues.detail: test_deprecated_redirected verifies the warning fires and that output still flows. Fine, but it locks in the old shape for the remaining release. Consider whether the test should only assert the warning, not re-validate the redirect semantics — the latter is essential complexity of code about to be deleted.

review.summary: This is a small, correct simplification: a homegrown context manager that complected two independent redirections is being retired in favor of two decomposable stdlib pieces. The diff is the right direction — less code, fewer incidental abstractions, time semantics unchanged. Two minor notes: the deprecation message should tell users how to replace the combined-streams case (the only thing the wrapper made "easy"), and the new test arguably over-specifies behavior of code marked for deletion. Overall SIMPLE, with one small EASY-NOT-SIMPLE residue in the migration guidance.
